title: Patterns and Processes in Inheritance

lessons.title: Genes, alleles, genotype and phenotype
lessons.question: How can the same gene be associated with different traits?
lessons.goal: Distinguish a gene from an allele, genotype from phenotype, and homozygous from heterozygous combinations.
lessons.prior: Homologous chromosomes carry corresponding genes but may carry different alleles. Gametes contribute one allele at each autosomal locus in the simple diploid model.

terms.meaning: A DNA sequence that contributes to a functional product or inherited characteristic.
terms.example: A DNA region influences a pigment-producing process.
terms.importantDistinction: A gene and a particular version of that gene are different concepts.
terms.misconception: A gene is always an entire chromosome.

terms.meaning: An alternative version of a gene.
terms.example: Two versions at the same locus are represented as B and b.
terms.importantDistinction: A diploid individual usually carries two alleles at an autosomal locus, even when more exist in the population.
terms.misconception: Each allele is a different chromosome set.

terms.meaning: The allele combination an organism carries at the locus or loci being considered.
terms.example: A model organism is Bb for a pigment gene.
terms.importantDistinction: Genotype records the allele combination, not just the appearance.
terms.misconception: Genotype means only visible appearance.

terms.meaning: An observable or measurable characteristic resulting from genotype and its biological context.
terms.example: A model organism produces dark pigment.
terms.importantDistinction: Phenotypes can include physiological or behavioural traits, not only colour.
terms.misconception: Phenotype is always a pair of letters.

sections: Start with a defined genetic model

A gene is a DNA sequence associated with a functional product or characteristic. Alternative versions are alleles. In a diploid autosomal model, an individual inherits one allele from each parent and therefore has two alleles at the locus being studied.

The genotype is the allele combination, such as BB, Bb or bb. The phenotype is the observed or measured characteristic, such as dark or pale pigment. A phenotype can also be an enzyme activity or another physiological property, not only a visible feature.
Dominance describes the heterozygote

Suppose a stated model says B gives dark pigment and is completely dominant to b. BB and Bb individuals have the dark phenotype, while bb individuals have the pale phenotype. The same phenotype can therefore correspond to more than one genotype.

Homozygous means the two alleles are the same, as in BB or bb. Heterozygous means they differ, as in Bb. A dominant allele is expressed in the heterozygote under the stated complete-dominance model. Dominant does not mean most common, healthiest or strongest.

Use the inheritance model supplied. Many traits involve multiple genes, environmental influences or allele relationships other than complete dominance. Do not assume that human eye colour can be accurately predicted by a single B/b model.
Notation keeps the reasoning visible

Define letters before solving a problem. Use the same letter for alleles of one gene and a different letter for a different gene. A capital and lowercase letter are convenient for a complete-dominance model; other models use different notation.

A useful first question is whether the phenotype determines a unique genotype. A recessive phenotype in a simple fully expressed model identifies bb. A dominant phenotype alone leaves BB or Bb possible. Keeping that uncertainty visible prevents an incorrect cross from the start.

lessons.title: Mendel’s experiments and segregation
lessons.question: How can a trait disappear in one generation and reappear in the next?
lessons.goal: Use P, F1 and F2 crosses to explain segregation of alleles without blending or loss of a recessive allele.
lessons.prior: A heterozygote carries two different alleles. Under complete dominance, only one corresponding phenotype is apparent.

terms.meaning: The separation of the two alleles at a locus into different gametes.
terms.example: A heterozygous Rr parent produces R and r gametes in the simple model.
terms.importantDistinction: The parent has both alleles, but an individual gamete receives one.
terms.misconception: Every gamete receives both R and r.

terms.meaning: Producing offspring with the same trait when bred within the line under the stated conditions.
terms.example: A homozygous pea line repeatedly produces the same flower phenotype.
terms.importantDistinction: In Mendel’s simple models, true-breeding lines are homozygous for the studied trait.
terms.misconception: True-breeding always means heterozygous.

terms.meaning: The first offspring generation from a specified parental cross.
terms.example: RR crossed with rr produces a first generation of Rr offspring.
terms.importantDistinction: F1 names a relationship to a cross, not a universal genotype.
terms.misconception: Every F1 individual in every cross is homozygous.

terms.meaning: The generation produced from the F1 in the specified breeding design.
terms.example: Two F1 heterozygotes are crossed to examine the next generation.
terms.importantDistinction: Its ratios depend on the parental genotypes and assumptions.
terms.misconception: Every F2 cross must yield exactly three offspring of one type and one of another.

sections: Follow the alleles across generations

Mendel studied traits in pea plants and used controlled crosses between lines with contrasting forms. In a simple example, let R represent round seeds and r wrinkled seeds, with complete dominance of R. A true-breeding RR line crossed with rr produces Rr offspring in the F1 generation.
Every F1 individual can have the round phenotype while still carrying the r allele. The recessive allele has not disappeared or blended into a weaker version. It remains part of the genotype.
Segregation explains reappearance
An Rr individual forms gametes containing R or r. The alleles segregate as homologous chromosomes separate during meiosis. In the simple model, each allele has a one-half chance of entering a gamete.

When two Rr individuals produce the F2 generation, gametes can combine as RR, Rr, rR or rr. Rr and rR name the same heterozygous genotype. The expected genotype ratio is 1 RR : 2 Rr : 1 rr. With complete dominance, the expected phenotype ratio is 3 round : 1 wrinkled.
The wrinkled phenotype reappears because an offspring can receive r from both parents. No new r mutation is required to explain that result.
Expected ratios are probabilities

A 3:1 expected ratio is not a promise that every group of four offspring contains exactly three round and one wrinkled. Each offspring is another event. Chance variation is especially noticeable in small samples.

Mendel's repeated patterns supported a particulate model of inheritance: inherited units remain distinguishable rather than permanently blending. Later chromosome and DNA evidence connected those units with cellular mechanisms.

When interpreting a cross, identify the parental genotypes, gamete possibilities and allele combinations before applying the phenotype rule. A remembered ratio should be the result of that reasoning, not a substitute for it.

lessons.title: Single-trait crosses and probability
lessons.question: How do you turn parental genotypes into an offspring prediction?
lessons.goal: Construct and interpret a monohybrid Punnett square, distinguish genotype and phenotype probabilities, and state the denominator.
lessons.prior: Aa forms A and a gametes under ordinary segregation. Expected ratios describe probabilities, not fixed family sequences.

terms.meaning: A table combining possible parental gametes to organize offspring genotypes.
terms.example: Rows list one parent’s gametes and columns the other’s.
terms.importantDistinction: Each cell represents a possible combination, not a separate guaranteed offspring.
terms.misconception: Each Punnett-square box is one child that must be born.

terms.meaning: A cross between individuals heterozygous for one studied gene.
terms.example: Aa × Aa is used to examine segregation of one locus.
terms.importantDistinction: A single-trait cross is not always heterozygote × heterozygote.
terms.misconception: Every single-trait cross is Aa × Aa.

terms.meaning: The expected proportion of an outcome under specified conditions.
terms.example: One of four equally likely combinations is homozygous recessive.
terms.importantDistinction: Use the group asked about as the denominator.
terms.misconception: Probability is a guarantee of the next outcome.

terms.meaning: The predicted count obtained by multiplying a probability by the sample size.
terms.example: A probability of 0.25 in 80 offspring gives an expected count of 20.
terms.importantDistinction: An expected count need not equal an observed count.
terms.misconception: Expected and observed counts must always be identical.

sections: Write gametes, not whole parental genotypes, on the edges

A Punnett square organizes combinations of gametes. For Aa × aa, the first parent produces A or a gametes; the second produces only a. Place those gametes on the edges and combine one from each parent in each cell.

The resulting possibilities are Aa and aa in equal proportions. With complete dominance, half are expected to have the dominant phenotype and half the recessive phenotype. The square shows why the 1:1 ratio applies; a 3:1 ratio would be the wrong shortcut for this cross.
Count the outcome that was actually asked for

For Aa × Aa, the four equally likely combinations are AA, Aa, aA and aa. Grouping the two heterozygous combinations gives probabilities of 1/4 AA, 1/2 Aa and 1/4 aa. The dominant phenotype has probability 3/4 under complete dominance.

Genotype probability and phenotype probability therefore can differ. “Heterozygous” refers to two of the four combinations, while “dominant phenotype” includes three. Mark the requested group before choosing your numerator.
When converting to an expected number, multiply by the total. If 80 offspring each have a 1/4 chance of aa, the expected number is 80 × 0.25 = 20. The result is an expectation, not a promise.
Independent offspring do not compensate for earlier outcomes

In the simple model, one offspring's genotype does not force the next offspring to be different. If two Aa parents have several dominant-phenotype offspring, the modeled probability for the next offspring is still 1/4 recessive.

For specified independent events, multiply probabilities. Two recessive offspring in a row from Aa × Aa have probability 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16. Do not confuse this ordered event with “at least one recessive among two,” which asks for a different set of outcomes.
State assumptions such as complete dominance and ordinary segregation. They determine which genotype combinations count toward a phenotype.

lessons.title: Test crosses and unknown genotypes
lessons.question: What can offspring reveal about a parent with a dominant phenotype?
lessons.goal: Use a homozygous recessive tester to distinguish possible parental genotypes and explain uncertainty from small samples.
lessons.prior: A dominant phenotype can be AA or Aa. An aa offspring must receive a from both parents.

terms.meaning: A cross with a homozygous recessive individual used to investigate an unknown genotype.
terms.example: A dark B_ individual is crossed with a pale bb tester.
terms.importantDistinction: One recessive offspring can be informative; all dominant offspring in a small sample need not prove homozygosity.
terms.misconception: Any four dominant offspring prove the unknown parent is homozygous.

terms.meaning: Having two identical alleles at a locus.
terms.example: An individual is AA or aa rather than Aa.
terms.importantDistinction: Homozygous can be dominant or recessive.
terms.misconception: Homozygous always means dominant.

terms.meaning: Having two different alleles at a locus.
terms.example: An individual has one dominant and one recessive allele in a simple model.
terms.importantDistinction: A heterozygote can share a phenotype with a homozygous dominant individual.
terms.misconception: Heterozygous means having one chromosome in the entire cell.

terms.meaning: Differences between observed sample outcomes and their expected proportions due to chance.
terms.example: A small set of offspring contains no recessive individual even though each had a one-half chance.
terms.importantDistinction: A small sample may not distinguish two models decisively.
terms.misconception: Every difference from an expected ratio proves a new inheritance law.

sections: Choose a tester with a known contribution

An individual with a dominant phenotype may be AA or Aa. Crossing it with aa creates a useful test because the recessive tester can contribute only a. The phenotype of the offspring then provides evidence about the unknown parent's contribution.

If the unknown parent is AA, every offspring is expected to be Aa and show the dominant phenotype. If the unknown parent is Aa, the expected offspring are half Aa and half aa. A recessive offspring therefore demonstrates that the unknown parent contributed a, under the stated simple model.
Positive evidence and absence of evidence differ
One aa offspring from B_ × bb means the dominant-phenotype parent must carry the recessive allele, assuming the model, parentage and observations are correct. It is heterozygous.

By contrast, several dominant offspring do not logically prove the parent is homozygous. An Aa parent can, by chance, produce a run of A-bearing gametes. For four independent offspring in an Aa × aa cross, the probability that all show the dominant phenotype is (1/2)⁴ = 1/16.

More offspring with no recessive phenotype generally strengthen the homozygous interpretation, but finite samples still require cautious wording. Say what the evidence supports and what remains possible.
Use family information before calculating

Additional parent or offspring information can resolve an unknown genotype. A dominant-phenotype individual with an aa parent must have received a from that parent, so it must be Aa. You do not need another test cross to establish that conclusion within the model.

Start with the most informative constraints. Write the alleles that must be present, preserve unknowns where necessary, and only then calculate the next cross. Guessing an unresolved genotype can make every later arithmetic step misleading.

lessons.title: Two-trait crosses and independent assortment
lessons.question: How do two single-gene predictions combine?
lessons.goal: List valid gametes for two loci, use a Punnett square or product rule, and identify the assumption of independent assortment.
lessons.prior: Each gamete receives one allele at each studied locus. Independent probabilities can be multiplied.

terms.meaning: A cross between individuals heterozygous at two studied loci.
terms.example: AaBb × AaBb is used to examine two traits under stated assumptions.
terms.importantDistinction: The familiar 9:3:3:1 phenotype ratio needs complete dominance and independent assortment.
terms.misconception: Every two-trait cross yields 9:3:3:1.

terms.meaning: Independent segregation of alleles at different loci when the chromosome arrangement permits it.
terms.example: An AaBb individual produces AB, Ab, aB and ab equally in an unlinked model.
terms.importantDistinction: Linked genes can depart from this equal-combination prediction.
terms.misconception: All genes always assort independently regardless of location.

terms.meaning: Multiplication of probabilities for specified independent events.
terms.example: Probability of aa and bb is calculated as P(aa) × P(bb) when the loci assort independently.
terms.importantDistinction: Check independence before multiplying separate trait probabilities.
terms.misconception: Probabilities of two required independent events are always added.

terms.meaning: The set of one allele from each studied locus carried by a gamete.
terms.example: An AaBb parent can produce an Ab gamete in an independent model.
terms.importantDistinction: A gamete does not receive both A and a at the same autosomal locus in this model.
terms.misconception: Aa is a valid normal two-locus gamete from AaBb.

sections: Find possible gametes before drawing boxes

For AaBb with independent assortment, choose one allele from the A/a pair and one from the B/b pair. The possible gametes are AB, Ab, aB and ab, each with probability 1/4. An Aabb parent has only Ab and ab as distinct possibilities.

Do not place Aa or Bb on a gamete edge. Those are two alleles of one locus, not one allele from each of two loci. A correctly sized square follows from the distinct gametes, not from a rule that every two-trait cross needs sixteen boxes.
Solve separate loci when independence is stated

For AaBb × AaBb, the A locus gives a 3/4 dominant-phenotype probability and 1/4 recessive probability. The B locus gives the same. If the loci assort independently, the probability of both dominant phenotypes is 3/4 × 3/4 = 9/16.
The other phenotype combinations are 3/16, 3/16 and 1/16, producing the familiar 9:3:3:1 expectation. This ratio is specific to the stated heterozygote cross and allele relationships.
For a different cross, recompute. In AaBb × aaBb, probability of A_ is 1/2 and probability of B_ is 3/4, so both dominant phenotypes have probability 3/8. A memorized 9/16 would be wrong.
Make the assumption part of the answer

Genes close together on the same chromosome can be linked. Their gamete combinations may not occur equally, so the simple product calculation can fail. Later lessons will use offspring data to test this.

For now, state when independent assortment is assumed. Check that the probabilities of all mutually exclusive phenotype categories add to one. When calculating an expected count, multiply the appropriate probability by the total number of offspring.
Both the square and product method are tools for organizing the same biological possibilities. Choose the clearer method, but show enough steps that the allele contributions can be checked.

lessons.title: Incomplete dominance and codominance
lessons.question: How can a heterozygote differ from either homozygote?
lessons.goal: Compare incomplete dominance and codominance while preserving ordinary allele segregation.
lessons.prior: An inheritance model determines the phenotype of a heterozygote; segregation still gives each gamete one allele.

terms.meaning: An allele relationship in which the heterozygote has an intermediate phenotype.
terms.example: Red and white flower alleles produce pink flowers in the specified heterozygote model.
terms.importantDistinction: An intermediate phenotype does not mean the alleles permanently blend.
terms.misconception: Incomplete dominance permanently blends the alleles into a new allele.

terms.meaning: An allele relationship in which both allele-associated products or traits are expressed in a heterozygote.
terms.example: A roan coat contains both red and white hairs in the model.
terms.importantDistinction: Codominance is not limited to separate patches of cells; both products can be present in the same cells.
terms.misconception: Codominance always means an intermediate blended phenotype.

terms.meaning: The characteristic expressed when two different alleles occur together.
terms.example: R1R2 may be pink in one model but red-and-white in another.
terms.importantDistinction: The same notation does not establish the inheritance relationship without its definition.
terms.misconception: Every heterozygote has the dominant homozygote phenotype.

terms.meaning: The expected relative proportions of expressed trait categories.
terms.example: An incomplete-dominance heterozygote cross gives three distinguishable phenotype categories.
terms.importantDistinction: Phenotype ratios can change even when genotype segregation is unchanged.
terms.misconception: Every heterozygote cross has a 3:1 phenotype ratio.

sections: The alleles still segregate

Under incomplete dominance, the heterozygote has an intermediate phenotype. In a stated flower model, R1R1 is red, R2R2 is white and R1R2 is pink. The alleles remain R1 and R2; they have not permanently fused into a pink allele.

Crossing two pink R1R2 plants gives R1R1, R1R2, R2R1 and R2R2 combinations. Grouped genotypes occur in a 1:2:1 ratio. Because all three genotypes have distinguishable phenotypes, the phenotype ratio is also 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white.
Both expressed is different from intermediate

In codominance, both allele-associated products or characteristics are expressed in the heterozygote. In a roan cattle model, red and white hairs are both present rather than becoming uniformly pink hair. In ABO blood groups, both A and B antigens can be expressed on red blood cells.

Do not define codominance only as different cells expressing different alleles. The essential idea is detectable expression of both allele contributions. The way that expression appears depends on the trait.
Use superscripts or clear allele labels such as R1 and R2 when neither allele is treated as completely dominant. Define the notation before interpreting the cross.
Change the phenotype rule, not the whole inheritance process

Punnett-square construction works the same way: list one allele per gamete, combine the possibilities, then use the specified genotype-to-phenotype rule. The difference from complete dominance lies in the heterozygote's phenotype.

A 1:2:1 genotype ratio can therefore produce either a 3:1 phenotype ratio under complete dominance or a 1:2:1 phenotype ratio when the three genotypes are distinguishable. The ratio alone must be read alongside the model.
Avoid calling one relationship “stronger” or “more advanced.” These are descriptions of expression, not rankings of alleles.

worked.title: Compare the same genotype cross under two models
worked.scenario: R1R2 × R1R2 is used in one incomplete-dominance flower model and one codominant coat-colour model.
steps: The genotype probabilities are 1/4 R1R1, 1/2 R1R2 and 1/4 R2R2 in both.
In incomplete dominance, the heterozygote is intermediate, such as pink.
In codominance, both contributions are expressed, such as red and white hairs.
The allele-segregation calculation stays the same; the interpretation of R1R2 changes.

guided.prompt: In an incomplete-dominance model, pink R1R2 × white R2R2 gives what fraction pink?
guided.explanation: The first parent contributes R1 or R2; the second only R2.
guided.cue: Write the two distinct combinations.

guided.prompt: Which observation best illustrates codominance in the stated coat model?
guided.explanation: Both contributions are distinguishable rather than intermediate.
guided.cue: Separate “both present” from “between the two.”

check.prompt: Why can white flowers reappear after crossing two pink incomplete-dominance heterozygotes?
check.answer: The white-associated alleles remain distinct and can combine in a homozygote
wrong: The pink allele must mutate back every generation
check.explanation: The alleles were not permanently blended.
check.cue: Trace the normal mechanism before choosing an answer.

check.prompt: Which statement correctly compares genotype and phenotype ratios for an R1R2 × R1R2 incomplete-dominance cross?
check.answer: Both are 1:2:1 when all three phenotypes are distinct
check.explanation: The heterozygote forms a separate phenotype category.
check.cue: Trace the normal mechanism before choosing an answer.

writing.prompt: Distinguish incomplete dominance from codominance with an explicitly defined example.
writing.model: Incomplete dominance produces an intermediate heterozygote phenotype, such as pink R1R2 flowers between red and white homozygotes. Codominance expresses both contributions, such as a roan coat with red and white hairs. In both models, the alleles remain distinct and segregate.

writing.model: A 3:1 phenotype ratio requires complete dominance, which groups the heterozygote with one homozygote. If the heterozygote is distinguishable, as in incomplete dominance or the specified codominance model, there are three phenotype categories in a 1:2:1 ratio.
criteria: Identifies the relevant structures or quantities.
Explains the causal relationship or calculation, not just the final result.
Uses the stated evidence and avoids a stronger conclusion than it supports.

applications.explanation: The R1R1 parent cannot contribute R2, so no offspring can receive two R2 alleles.
applications.cue: Trace the normal mechanism before choosing an answer.

self: Do incomplete dominance and codominance cancel Mendel’s segregation rule?
No. They change how allele combinations are expressed, not the one-allele contribution of each gamete.

lessons.title: Multiple alleles and ABO blood groups
lessons.question: How can a population have three alleles when one person has two?
lessons.goal: Use the ABO model to distinguish population allele diversity from individual genotype and solve blood-group crosses.
lessons.prior: Codominance allows both allele contributions to be expressed. A diploid individual usually has two alleles at one autosomal locus.

terms.meaning: More than two allele versions of one gene present in a population.
terms.example: The simplified ABO model includes IA, IB and i.
terms.importantDistinction: An individual still usually carries only two alleles at that autosomal locus.
terms.misconception: Multiple alleles means every person carries three ABO alleles.

terms.meaning: A blood-group system modeled with IA, IB and i alleles producing A, B, AB and O phenotypes.
terms.example: IAIB expresses both A and B antigen types.
terms.importantDistinction: The classroom model omits rare variants and is not a transfusion decision tool.
terms.misconception: ABO group alone is enough for every clinical transfusion decision.

terms.meaning: Alleles whose contributions are both expressed in the heterozygote.
terms.example: IA and IB are both expressed in the IAIB genotype.
terms.importantDistinction: Both are dominant over i in the simplified ABO model.
terms.misconception: IA must completely mask IB.

terms.meaning: An individual who carries a recessive disease-associated allele without expressing the recessive condition in a specified simple model.
terms.example: A heterozygote passes a recessive allele to offspring while showing the dominant phenotype.
terms.importantDistinction: Use carrier only when the inheritance model and trait make the meaning appropriate.
terms.misconception: Every person with a dominant disease allele is an unaffected carrier.

sections: Population diversity is not individual copy number

A population can contain many versions of a gene. Each diploid individual still usually inherits two alleles at an autosomal locus, one from each parent. Multiple alleles refers to the range of versions in the population, not three or more copies in every individual.

The simplified ABO model uses IA, IB and i. IA contributes A antigen expression; IB contributes B antigen expression; i does not produce either A or B antigen in this model. IA and IB are codominant, and each is dominant over i.
Connect each phenotype to possible genotypes

Type A can be IAIA or IAi. Type B can be IBIB or IBi. Type AB is IAIB, and type O is ii in the standard model. The phenotypes A and B leave genotype uncertainty unless additional family information is available.
An individual with type B and a type O parent must have inherited i from that parent. Therefore the type B individual's genotype is IBi. This is the same constraint reasoning used in a test cross.
Use clear notation. IAIB represents two alleles of one gene, not four separate genes. In plain text, write IA and IB consistently and keep the allele pairs grouped.
Calculate from the actual cross
For IAi × IBi, possible offspring genotypes are IAIB, IAi, IBi and ii, each with probability 1/4. The four ABO phenotypes are therefore each possible with probability 1/4 in this specific cross.
A different cross gives different predictions. IAIA × IBi produces IAIB and IAi, each with probability 1/2; no ii offspring is possible because the first parent cannot contribute i.

These models teach inheritance and probability. Real blood typing includes additional factors and rare variants. Do not use a classroom square as a clinical transfusion rule or as definitive proof of family relationships.

worked.title: Use family information before the square
worked.scenario: A type B parent has a type O father. This parent has a child with a type AB partner. Find the probability of type O.
steps: The type O father is ii and supplies i, so the type B parent is IBi.
The AB partner is IAIB and can supply IA or IB, but not i.
An O child would require ii.
Because one parent cannot supply i, the probability is 0 in the simplified model.

guided.prompt: What genotype corresponds to type AB?
guided.explanation: Both antigen-associated alleles are present and expressed.
guided.cue: AB represents codominant expression, not a recessive allele.

guided.prompt: For IAi × ii, what fraction is type O?
guided.explanation: The combinations are IAi and ii equally.
guided.cue: The ii parent always supplies i.

check.prompt: Which statement correctly describes multiple alleles?
check.answer: A population can have more than two alleles while an individual carries two
wrong: Every individual must carry every population allele
Each allele belongs to a different chromosome type
check.explanation: Population diversity and diploid allele count are separate.
check.cue: Trace the normal mechanism before choosing an answer.

check.prompt: For IAi × IBi, what is the probability of type AB?
check.explanation: Only the IA × IB combination gives IAIB among four equally likely combinations.
check.cue: Trace the normal mechanism before choosing an answer.

writing.prompt: List the ABO genotypes in the simplified model and explain the dominance relationships.
writing.model: Type A is IAIA or IAi, type B is IBIB or IBi, type AB is IAIB, and type O is ii. IA and IB are codominant with one another and each is dominant over i.
criteria: Identifies the relevant structures or quantities.
Explains the causal relationship or calculation, not just the final result.
Uses the stated evidence and avoids a stronger conclusion than it supports.

writing.prompt: A type A individual has a type O parent and a type O partner. Determine the possible offspring groups and show the reasoning.
writing.model: The type O parent supplied i, so the type A individual is IAi. The partner is ii. IAi × ii produces IAi and ii with equal probability, giving expected type A and type O offspring in a 1:1 ratio.
criteria: Identifies the relevant structures or quantities.
Explains the causal relationship or calculation, not just the final result.
Uses the stated evidence and avoids a stronger conclusion than it supports.

applications.prompt: A type AB parent and a type O parent have a child. Which groups are possible in the standard model?
applications.explanation: IAIB × ii produces IAi or IBi, not IAIB or ii.
applications.cue: Trace the normal mechanism before choosing an answer.

self: Does type A reveal whether the individual is IAIA or IAi?
Not by itself. Family information or other evidence may be needed.

lessons.title: Sex-linked inheritance
lessons.question: Why does “an affected son” differ from “an affected child”?
lessons.goal: Use a typical XX/XY model to solve X-linked crosses and distinguish conditional from joint probabilities.
lessons.prior: The denominator must match the group asked about. Each gamete contributes one sex chromosome in the typical model.

terms.meaning: Located on the X chromosome.
terms.example: An allele is represented as Xb rather than as an autosomal b alone.
terms.importantDistinction: An XY individual has only one allele at many X-linked loci.
terms.misconception: X-linked alleles are normally passed on the Y chromosome.

terms.meaning: Having only one copy of a gene in the relevant chromosome context.
terms.example: A typical XY individual has one copy of many X-linked genes.
terms.importantDistinction: Hemizygous is not the same as homozygous.
terms.misconception: An XY individual is homozygous at every X-linked locus.

terms.meaning: Probability calculated within a stated subgroup or condition.
terms.example: The question asks what fraction of sons are affected, not what fraction of all children are affected sons.
terms.importantDistinction: Changing the denominator can change the numerical answer.
terms.misconception: Among sons and among all children always give the same probability.

terms.meaning: An inheritance model in which the recessive allele is on X and is expressed in a hemizygous XY individual.
terms.example: A carrier XX parent can have an affected XY offspring.
terms.importantDistinction: An affected father does not transmit his X to sons in the typical XX/XY model.
terms.misconception: Affected fathers pass their X-linked allele to every son.

sections: Keep alleles attached to their chromosomes

Use X superscripts or clear plain-text forms such as XB and Xb. In a typical XX/XY model, an XX parent contributes an X to every offspring; an XY parent contributes X or Y. Many X-linked loci have no corresponding allele on Y.

For a simple X-linked recessive condition, XbY expresses the condition because there is no second X-linked allele to mask it. XBXb can be an unaffected carrier under the stated complete-expression assumptions, while XbXb is affected. These are inheritance models, not a complete account of every variation in sex development or gene expression.
Use the cross to find the correct denominator
Consider XBXb × XBY. The four equally likely combinations are XBXB, XBXb, XBY and XbY. One of four children is expected to be affected. Among sons only, one of two is expected to be affected.

The probability of “a son who is affected” is 1/4 among all children. The probability that “the next son is affected” is 1/2 conditional on being a son. The wording changes the denominator, not the biological cross.

An affected father passes his X chromosome to daughters and his Y to sons in this model. Father-to-son transmission therefore is not expected for an X-linked allele through that direct chromosome path.
Separate recessive and dominant X-linked models

For a simple fully penetrant X-linked dominant trait, an affected father with an unaffected partner passes his affected X to every daughter and to no son. An affected heterozygous mother can pass the allele to either sons or daughters.

These patterns are useful evidence, but a small family may not contain every possible outcome. Later pedigree lessons will require testing candidate explanations against the whole family rather than treating one clue as proof.
Always define allele meaning, parental genotypes and the subgroup asked about before calculating.

worked.title: Answer two similar-looking questions
worked.scenario: A carrier XAXa mother and unaffected XAY father have children in a simple X-linked recessive model.
steps: List the four equally likely combinations: XAXA, XAXa, XAY and XaY.
Affected child: XaY is one of four, so probability = 1/4.
Affected among sons: XaY is one of two son outcomes, so probability = 1/2.
A son who is affected among all children: probability remains 1/4.
Write the denominator in words to show which question you answered.

guided.prompt: For XAXa × XAY, what fraction of daughters is affected?
guided.explanation: Every daughter receives XA from the father in this recessive model.
guided.cue: Restrict the denominator to the daughter combinations.

guided.prompt: Which sex chromosome does a father transmit to a son in the typical model?
guided.explanation: A son receives the paternal Y and a maternal X.
guided.cue: Trace the direct chromosome contribution.

check.prompt: For XaXa × XAY in a recessive model, what fraction of sons is affected?
check.explanation: Every son receives Xa from the mother and Y from the father.
check.cue: Trace the normal mechanism before choosing an answer.

check.prompt: For XAXa × XAY, what is the probability of the next child being an affected son?
check.explanation: Only XaY is both a son and affected among the four equal combinations.
check.cue: Trace the normal mechanism before choosing an answer.

writing.prompt: Explain the difference between “probability an offspring is an affected son” and “probability a son is affected.” Use a carrier mother and unaffected father.
writing.model: For XAXa × XAY, one of four total offspring combinations is an affected son, so the joint probability is 1/4. Among the two son combinations, one is affected, giving a conditional probability of 1/2. The denominator differs.
criteria: Identifies the relevant structures or quantities.
Explains the causal relationship or calculation, not just the final result.
Uses the stated evidence and avoids a stronger conclusion than it supports.

writing.prompt: Explain why an affected father does not directly pass an X-linked allele to his sons in the typical XX/XY model.
writing.model: Sons receive the father’s Y chromosome, not his X. The paternal X goes to daughters. Therefore direct father-to-son transmission does not occur through an X-linked locus in this model.
criteria: Identifies the relevant structures or quantities.
Explains the causal relationship or calculation, not just the final result.
Uses the stated evidence and avoids a stronger conclusion than it supports.

applications.prompt: A father has a fully penetrant X-linked dominant trait and the mother is unaffected. What is expected for daughters?
applications.answer: All inherit the affected paternal X
wrong: Exactly half inherit the father’s Y
applications.explanation: Every daughter receives the father’s X in the typical model.
applications.cue: Trace the normal mechanism before choosing an answer.

self: Why should an X-linked cross retain X and Y in the notation?
They show which allele is carried on which chromosome and make sex-specific probabilities traceable.

lessons.title: Polygenic traits and environmental influences
lessons.question: Why do many traits vary continuously instead of falling into two groups?
lessons.goal: Explain polygenic and environmental contributions, and distinguish genotype, gene expression and measured phenotype.
lessons.prior: Single-locus squares are simplified models. A phenotype need not be controlled by only one gene.

terms.meaning: Inheritance in which multiple genes contribute to a trait.
terms.example: Several gene regions contribute to variation in height.
terms.importantDistinction: Polygenic does not mean many alleles at only one locus.
terms.misconception: Polygenic inheritance and multiple alleles are identical terms.

terms.meaning: A range of phenotype values without only a few sharply separated categories.
terms.example: A class has a range of measured heights rather than only tall and short genotypes.
terms.importantDistinction: Continuous measurements can reflect both genetic and environmental contributions.
terms.misconception: Continuous variation means genes have no influence.

terms.meaning: An effect of conditions such as nutrition or temperature on phenotype.
terms.example: Plants with similar genotypes grow to different sizes under different resource conditions.
terms.importantDistinction: An environmental effect does not necessarily change the inherited DNA sequence.
terms.misconception: Every environmental effect on phenotype is a DNA mutation.

terms.meaning: Use of genetic information to produce functional products in cells.
terms.example: Cells make different proteins under different developmental or environmental conditions.
terms.importantDistinction: Expression can change without changing the allele sequence.
terms.misconception: Possessing an allele guarantees identical expression in every cell and condition.

sections: Several genes can contribute to one measurement

A polygenic trait is influenced by multiple genes. Different allele combinations across these loci can produce a range of outcomes. Human height and many aspects of pigmentation are examples of traits that are not adequately represented by one complete-dominance pair.

Continuous variation describes measurements spread over a range. It does not require every possible value, nor does it prove that environment is the only influence. Many gene combinations and environmental conditions can together generate a broad distribution.
The environment affects expression and development

Nutrition, temperature and other conditions can influence a phenotype. Plants with similar genotypes may reach different heights under different light or nutrient conditions. The measured difference does not automatically establish a difference in DNA sequence.

Gene expression describes which genetic information is used and how much product is made. Cells with the same inherited genome can have different functions because they express different sets of genes. Environmental or developmental signals can change expression.

Some regulatory changes involve chemical modifications associated with DNA or chromatin. These are often discussed as epigenetic changes. Do not treat every such change as a mutation or assume it is always inherited through many generations.
Ask what the evidence separates

If two groups differ in both genotype and environment, a phenotype difference cannot be assigned to either factor alone without additional evidence. Controlled comparisons hold relevant conditions constant or use designs that help separate contributions.

A genetic association can indicate a relationship without determining an individual outcome with certainty. Many traits and conditions involve multiple factors. The existence of a risk-associated allele is not equivalent to an inevitable phenotype.

For a course answer, name the proposed contributions, identify what was measured and explain the limit. Avoid forcing a complex trait into a single-gene square just because that calculation is familiar.

worked.title: Interpret an environmental comparison
worked.scenario: Genetically similar cuttings are grown under high or low light, with other measured conditions kept similar. Their average growth differs.
steps: The genetic similarity reduces one source of variation.
The light condition differs systematically, so it is a plausible contributor.
The result concerns growth under those conditions; it does not prove a new allele appeared.
Check replication and other controlled conditions before making a stronger causal claim.

wrong: Multiple alleles at one locus only
guided.explanation: Polygenic refers to contributions from multiple genes.
guided.cue: Count contributing loci, not versions of one gene.

guided.explanation: Cells can use different genetic information without having unrelated genomes.
guided.cue: Separate possession of DNA from use of DNA.

check.answer: Multiple alleles concern one locus; polygenic inheritance involves multiple loci
wrong: Both terms always mean three chromosome sets
Multiple alleles occur only in haploid organisms
check.explanation: Allele diversity within a locus differs from the number of loci contributing to a trait.
check.cue: Trace the normal mechanism before choosing an answer.

check.answer: A difference exists, but its separate causes need more evidence
wrong: The cause must be entirely genetic
The cause must be entirely environmental
A single dominant allele explains every individual
check.explanation: Confounded differences do not isolate one cause.
check.cue: Trace the normal mechanism before choosing an answer.

writing.model: Multiple genes can contribute different effects, and environmental conditions can influence expression and development. Many combinations produce a range of measurements. A single complete-dominance Punnett square is therefore not an adequate model for every trait.

Explains the causal relationship or calculation, not just the final result.

writing.model: A gene-expression change affects how genetic information is used or how much product is produced. The allele sequence can remain unchanged. A mutation changes the DNA sequence itself. Either can influence phenotype, but they are not the same process.

Explains the causal relationship or calculation, not just the final result.
Uses the stated evidence and avoids a stronger conclusion than it supports.

applications.answer: Phenotype changed through a non-sequence environmental effect
wrong: The organism has no genes for pigment
Its chromosome number must have doubled
applications.explanation: Phenotype can change through expression or biochemical conditions without sequence change.

No. Penetrance, environment and other genetic factors can influence the outcome.

lessons.title: Reading autosomal pedigrees
lessons.question: How do family relationships constrain possible genotypes?
lessons.goal: Read pedigree symbols and generations, infer autosomal genotypes under a stated model, and preserve unresolved alternatives.
lessons.prior: An affected phenotype means different genotypes in dominant and recessive models. Define the model before assigning letters.

terms.meaning: A diagram tracing a specified trait through family relationships across generations.
terms.example: Symbols connected by parent–offspring lines show which relatives express a trait.
terms.importantDistinction: A pedigree is evidence to test a model, not proof that one clue is always decisive.
terms.misconception: One affected symbol proves the inheritance mode.

terms.meaning: A model in which a trait is expressed when two recessive alleles occur at an autosomal locus.
terms.example: Two unaffected Aa parents can have an affected aa child.
terms.importantDistinction: Unaffected individuals can be AA or Aa.
terms.misconception: All unaffected individuals must be AA.

terms.meaning: A model in which one dominant allele at an autosomal locus is sufficient for expression under the stated assumptions.
terms.example: An affected Dd individual and unaffected dd partner can have affected or unaffected children.
terms.importantDistinction: Affected individuals can be DD or Dd unless other evidence resolves the genotype.
terms.misconception: Every affected dominant individual must be DD.

terms.meaning: A level of descent in a family diagram, commonly labelled with a Roman numeral.
terms.example: I, II and III distinguish successive levels in a pedigree.
terms.importantDistinction: Individual numbers identify people within a generation.
terms.misconception: The Roman numeral gives the person’s chromosome count.

sections: Read the diagram before solving it

A pedigree uses symbols and connecting lines to represent family relationships and a specified trait. Conventional squares and circles often represent male and female individuals in the model; shading indicates expression of the trait. A key should explain any additional symbols.

Roman numerals identify generations and ordinary numbers identify individuals within a generation. A label such as II-3 refers to the third numbered individual in generation II. Follow the parent–offspring line carefully; neighbouring symbols are not automatically siblings or partners.
Use required allele contributions

For an autosomal recessive model, affected individuals are aa. Two unaffected parents with an affected child must each contribute a. If both are unaffected, each is therefore Aa under the simple fully penetrant model.

For an autosomal dominant model, unaffected individuals are dd. An affected parent with an unaffected child must be able to contribute d, so that affected parent is Dd rather than DD. The child's genotype constrains the parent's possible alleles.

These deductions use the stated model, accurate relationships and complete expression. New mutations, reduced penetrance or other complexities can change the interpretation; do not add them silently to a simple problem.
Leave uncertainty where it belongs

An unaffected sibling of an aa child from Aa × Aa can be AA or Aa. Excluding aa leaves three equally likely genotype combinations: AA, Aa and aA. Therefore the probability that an unaffected sibling is a carrier is 2/3, not 1/2, under this cross.
Do not assign AA simply because a person is unshaded. Write the allowed alternatives unless other evidence resolves them. The distinction between “must be” and “could be” is important.
A pedigree can make some genotypes certain within a model while leaving others unresolved. A good explanation identifies the relative whose allele contribution provides the evidence.

worked.title: Infer both parents from a recessive child
worked.scenario: Two unaffected parents have an affected child in a fully penetrant autosomal recessive model.
steps: The affected child is aa and needs a from each parent.
Each unaffected parent must also carry A.
Therefore both parents are Aa.
An unaffected sibling may be AA or Aa; do not automatically mark that sibling as a carrier.
Conditional on being unaffected, the carrier probability is 2/3 for this parental cross.

guided.explanation: Two recessive alleles are required in this simple model.
guided.cue: Define affected before reading the shading.

guided.prompt: An affected dominant parent has an unaffected dd child. What must that parent be?
guided.explanation: The parent must contribute d but also carry D to be affected.
guided.cue: Use the child’s required allele contribution.

check.explanation: Removing aa leaves AA, Aa and aA; two of three are carriers.

check.answer: They may be a heterozygous carrier
check.explanation: Both AA and Aa can be unaffected under the model.

writing.model: The child is aa and receives a from each parent. Because each parent is unaffected under the complete-penetrance recessive model, each must also have A. Thus both parents are Aa.

Explains the causal relationship or calculation, not just the final result.
Uses the stated evidence and avoids a stronger conclusion than it supports.

writing.model: An affected sibling must be aa. An unaffected sibling cannot be aa but may be AA or Aa. Without additional information, the specific genotype is unresolved; the conditional carrier probability is 2/3.
criteria: Identifies the relevant structures or quantities.
Explains the causal relationship or calculation, not just the final result.
Uses the stated evidence and avoids a stronger conclusion than it supports.

self: What does II-3 mean in a conventional pedigree?
Individual 3 in generation II, not three chromosomes in the second cell.

lessons.title: Sex-linked pedigrees and testing a model
lessons.question: How can you test an inheritance explanation against an entire family?
lessons.goal: Use chromosome transmission to evaluate X-linked models and distinguish consistency from proof in small pedigrees.
lessons.prior: In the typical XX/XY model, fathers pass X to daughters and Y to sons. A small family may not show every possible outcome.

terms.meaning: A simple model in which a dominant allele on X produces the trait under specified penetrance assumptions.
terms.example: An affected father transmits his affected X to all daughters in the typical model.
terms.importantDistinction: No direct paternal X is transmitted to a son.
terms.misconception: An affected father must pass his X-linked dominant allele to all sons.

terms.meaning: The proportion of individuals with a genotype who express the associated phenotype.
terms.example: A simple pedigree question assumes every person with a specified genotype expresses the trait.
terms.importantDistinction: Incomplete penetrance can make patterns less straightforward than classroom models.
terms.misconception: Penetrance is the number of chromosomes in a gamete.

terms.meaning: A possible inheritance explanation tested against the observed relationships and traits.
terms.example: An X-linked recessive hypothesis is checked for contradictions in every branch.
terms.importantDistinction: A model consistent with a small family need not be the only possible explanation.
terms.misconception: One matching clue proves a model uniquely.

terms.meaning: An individual who must carry a recessive allele under the stated pedigree model.
terms.example: An unaffected mother of an affected son carries the relevant X-linked recessive allele when other assumptions hold.
terms.importantDistinction: The conclusion depends on the model and relationship information.
terms.misconception: Every unaffected female in an X-linked pedigree is automatically a carrier.

sections: Trace the chromosome, not only the shading pattern

For X-linked inheritance, follow which parent supplies X to each offspring. Sons receive their X from their mother in the typical XX/XY model. Daughters receive one X from each parent. Fathers do not directly pass an X-linked allele to sons.

In a fully penetrant X-linked recessive model, an affected son has XbY. His Xb came from his mother. An unaffected mother must therefore be XBXb under the ordinary no-new-mutation assumptions. An affected daughter needs Xb from both parents, which constrains the father's genotype.
Compare dominant and recessive X-linked patterns

An affected father in an X-linked dominant model passes the affected X to every daughter. With an unaffected mother, sons receive the father's Y and the mother's unaffected X, so they are unaffected under that model.

For X-linked recessive inheritance, an affected father with a homozygous unaffected mother has carrier daughters and unaffected sons. The same chromosome route produces a different expressed pattern because the heterozygote phenotype differs.
More affected males can be a clue to an X-linked recessive model, but sex counts alone are not decisive. A small autosomal family can also show an uneven distribution by chance.
Look for contradictions and retain limits
A strong pedigree analysis tests every informative relationship. A model may fit one branch but fail elsewhere. Use “consistent with” when the evidence supports a model without uniquely proving it.

State assumptions: complete penetrance, ordinary chromosome transmission, accurate parentage and no newly arising mutations unless specified. These simplify the question and make deductions possible. Real clinical pedigrees can require more evidence.

When calculating the risk to a future child, establish the relevant parents' genotypes first and read the requested subgroup. The pedigree does not remove the distinction between probability among sons and probability among all children.

lessons.title: Linked genes and recombinant offspring
lessons.question: Why do some two-trait crosses depart from independent assortment?
lessons.goal: Identify linked allele arrangements, parental and recombinant combinations, and use a test cross to interpret gamete frequencies.
lessons.prior: Independent AaBb gametes are expected in equal proportions. Crossing over can exchange segments between homologues.

terms.meaning: Genes on the same chromosome that may be inherited together, especially when close.
terms.example: AB is carried on one homologue and ab on the other.
terms.importantDistinction: Physical linkage can reduce recombinant frequency, but widely separated loci may appear independent.
terms.misconception: Any genes on the same chromosome can never recombine.

terms.meaning: An allele combination matching one of the original chromosome arrangements in the heterozygous parent.
terms.example: For AB/ab, the combinations AB and ab are parental.
terms.importantDistinction: Parental depends on the specified phase, not always capital letters together.
terms.misconception: AB is always parental in every heterozygote.

terms.meaning: An allele combination different from the parent’s original arrangement for the loci considered.
terms.example: For AB/ab, crossing over can generate Ab and aB.
terms.importantDistinction: Recombinant does not necessarily mean a new allele was created.
terms.misconception: A recombinant always contains a novel mutation.

terms.meaning: The arrangement of alleles across the two homologous chromosomes.
terms.example: AB/ab differs from Ab/aB even though both can be written AaBb.

sections: A genotype can hide chromosome arrangement

AaBb tells you which alleles are present but not how they are arranged on the homologues. AB/ab places A with B on one chromosome and a with b on the other. Ab/aB places A with b and a with B. This arrangement is called linkage phase.

The original combinations are parental. Crossing over between the loci can generate recombinant combinations. Which combinations count as parental therefore depends on the starting arrangement, not simply whether the letters are both uppercase.
A test cross can reveal gamete combinations

Cross a heterozygote with aabb. The tester contributes only ab, so the offspring's phenotype or genotype can reveal the heterozygote's gamete contribution. Under independent assortment, the four combinations are expected in equal proportions.

If the heterozygote has AB/ab and the genes are linked, AB and ab gametes often occur more frequently than Ab and aB. The corresponding parental offspring classes are larger, and the recombinant classes smaller.
Read the actual counts, not just the presence of four categories. Linked genes can produce all four combinations if crossing over occurs, but the proportions can differ from 1:1:1:1.
Linkage is about probability, not an absolute lock

Closer genes are less likely to be separated by crossing over between them. Genes farther apart may show more recombination. Multiple crossovers can complicate the relationship between observed recombinant frequency and physical distance.
A small sample can depart from equal counts by chance, so a slight imbalance alone is not conclusive proof of linkage. Large, consistent differences provide stronger evidence under the stated model.
Keep the explanation at the correct level: crossing over changes combinations within chromosomes, and offspring counts can provide evidence about those gamete combinations.

lessons.title: Recombination frequency and chromosome maps
lessons.question: How can offspring counts estimate relative gene positions?
lessons.goal: Calculate recombination frequency, construct simple maps and distinguish map distance from a universal physical base-pair distance.
lessons.prior: Parental and recombinant classes depend on phase. Count both reciprocal recombinant classes.

terms.meaning: The fraction of scored offspring or gametes that are recombinant for the loci considered.
terms.example: Eighteen of 100 test-cross offspring are recombinant, giving 18%.
terms.importantDistinction: Use all scored offspring in the denominator and both recombinant classes in the numerator.
terms.misconception: Only the smallest recombinant class belongs in the numerator.

terms.meaning: A unit of genetic map distance corresponding approximately to one percent recombination over short intervals.
terms.example: A short interval with about 8% recombinants is estimated as about 8 map units.
terms.importantDistinction: A map unit is not a universal fixed number of base pairs.
terms.misconception: One map unit always equals exactly one million base pairs.

terms.meaning: A map of relative gene order and distances estimated from recombination data.
terms.example: Genes A, B and C are placed along a line with measured intervals.
terms.importantDistinction: A genetic map is not a direct microscopic measurement of DNA length.
terms.misconception: A linkage map is a photograph of the chromosome.

terms.meaning: Two exchange events within a chromosome region.
terms.example: Two exchanges can restore the original outside-marker arrangement.
terms.importantDistinction: Undetected multiple crossovers can make observed two-locus recombination underestimate longer distances.
terms.misconception: Two-locus recombination frequency increases without limit above 50%.

sections: Calculate the fraction carefully

Recombination frequency equals recombinant observations divided by total scored observations, multiplied by 100%. In a test cross, add both reciprocal recombinant classes. Do not divide only by the parental classes or by one quarter of the offspring.
For 84 parental class 1, 76 parental class 2, 22 recombinant class 1 and 18 recombinant class 2, the total is 200. Recombinants total 40. Frequency = 40/200 × 100% = 20%.
In a simple short-interval model, this suggests approximately 20 map units between the loci. The result is a relative genetic distance estimate, not an exact physical measurement.
Use three distances to infer order

Suppose A–B is 6 map units, B–C is 14 and A–C is 20 in a simple additive map. Since 6 + 14 = 20, B lies between A and C. Either A—6—B—14—C or its reversed orientation expresses the same relative order.

Two distances alone may leave more than one order possible. Place the genes tentatively and ask what additional comparison would distinguish the alternatives. Do not invent a third distance merely to finish the drawing.
Understand the limits of two-locus data

Observed recombination frequency approaches 50% for independently assorting loci or sufficiently separated loci. It does not provide an unbounded direct ruler. Multiple crossovers can restore parental outside-marker combinations, so some exchange events are not detected by scoring only two loci.

A chromosome map can span more than 50 map units when shorter intervals are combined, even though a two-locus recombination fraction does not rise above the independent limit in the standard model. These are different quantities.

The connection between centimorgans and base pairs varies across regions and organisms. Report the calculated genetic distance and assumptions, rather than converting every map unit into one fixed DNA length.

lessons.title: Genetic testing, counselling and decisions
lessons.question: What can genetic information tell a person—and what can it leave uncertain?
lessons.goal: Distinguish a genetic test result from a guaranteed phenotype, and identify consent, uncertainty and privacy considerations.
lessons.prior: Genotype does not determine every complex phenotype on its own. Pedigree conclusions rely on assumptions and available evidence.

terms.meaning: Analysis of genetic material or related markers to investigate particular variants or conditions.
terms.example: A test checks for a specified DNA variant.
terms.importantDistinction: A test’s scope determines what a negative or positive result can establish.
terms.misconception: A negative test rules out every genetic condition.

terms.meaning: A process helping people understand genetic information, inheritance and possible implications for their choices.
terms.example: A professional explains a result, its uncertainty and relevant family context.
terms.importantDistinction: Counselling supports informed decisions rather than dictating one choice for every family.
terms.misconception: Genetic counselling guarantees a particular future phenotype.

terms.meaning: Agreement based on understanding the purpose, potential benefits, risks and alternatives of a procedure or study.
terms.example: A participant considers how a genetic sample and results will be used before agreeing.
terms.importantDistinction: Consent involves more than the physical act of giving a sample.
terms.misconception: Providing a sample means agreeing to every future use automatically.

terms.meaning: A probability or increased likelihood associated with genetic information in a specified context.
terms.example: A variant is associated with increased probability of a condition without making it inevitable.
terms.importantDistinction: Risk is not the same as certainty.
terms.misconception: A risk-associated allele always causes the condition in every carrier.

sections: Read the scope of the test

A genetic test investigates particular variants, regions or markers. A result must be interpreted within that scope. A negative result for one variant does not rule out every genetic cause of a trait or condition.

Some results are strongly predictive under a clear inheritance model. Others indicate an increased probability or remain uncertain. Penetrance, other genes, environment and the quality of the evidence can influence what a result means for an individual.
Information can affect more than one person

A result can have implications for relatives because family members share some genetic information. A person may wish to know a result, decline it or discuss its meaning before deciding how to use it. Genetic counselling helps explain inheritance, limitations and possible implications.

Consent should address what is tested, what results may be returned and how samples or data may be used. Privacy and access to information are relevant concerns. This chapter examines those issues without giving legal advice or assuming one personal choice is appropriate for everyone.
A scientific explanation should separate observed data, estimated risk and value-based decisions. An association does not itself prescribe how a person should act.
Evaluate a claim using evidence and uncertainty

Suppose a hypothetical test reports a variant associated with a higher risk of a condition. Ask which population was studied, how large the increase is, what other factors matter and whether the result has been validated for the proposed use.

A claim that one result predicts every future feature of a person's health goes beyond the evidence. Conversely, uncertainty does not mean the information has no value. The useful task is to identify what the result can support and what additional evidence or counselling is needed.
Classroom case studies should not require students to reveal their own family history or test information. Use the supplied fictional scenarios for analysis.

A biobank stores biological samples and associated information for research. Comparing many samples can help investigate relationships between variants, environments and phenotypes.

sections: One method, several inheritance models

Begin with the gene or genes, the allele relationships and parental genotypes. Segregation determines the allele contribution of gametes; the phenotype model determines which offspring combinations express the trait. Complete dominance, incomplete dominance, codominance and X-linkage change how outcomes are interpreted.

A two-locus product calculation requires independence. A linked model instead uses phase and recombinant frequencies. A pedigree adds constraints from relatives but may leave more than one genotype or inheritance model possible.
Show the denominator and the limit

Probability among all children differs from probability among sons or among unaffected siblings. Count the requested subgroup explicitly. Multiply independent required events, and convert a probability to an expected count only after establishing the correct cross.
Expected ratios are not guarantees for small samples. Genetic associations are not always deterministic predictions. A complete answer gives both the result and the conditions under which it follows.
